verdicts.note: Exposure is teen pregnancy instrumented by menarche; outcome is schooling and labour supply. No living arrangement anywhere.
Sequence analysis of Italian pathways to adulthood; leaving the parental home is one transition among several and no fertility effect is estimated.
Tests directly whether co-residence of older parents with adult children of reproductive age raises the number of children, 11 European countries; finds no support.
Missing women; patrilocality appears as background to sex selection. A.10 / D.2.c.

Military enlistment after 9/11 with marriage and fertility outcomes. This is scope §4 design 4 in the wild, but the living arrangement is never measured, so the exposure is service, not the arrangement. Flagged as a candidate instrument for full-text follow-up.
Spatial RD on partible vs impartible inheritance; persistent effect on household SIZE and explicitly none on fertility. Link 1 with a null on link 2.
French cohabitation prevalence; no parental co-residence and no fertility estimate.
Parental influence on mate selection, 1953. Exposure is parental involvement, not the arrangement.
Age at return marriage against fertility in rural India; the parental home appears only as an explanation for long first-birth intervals. A.7's.
Stem-family headship transfer in rural Japan; the arrangement is the subject but there is no fertility outcome.
Freeway opinion survey; matched on 'number of children living at home' as a covariate.
Joint versus nuclear household type against fertility and authority, 1,022 Bombay families, by social class.
Cohort life-cycle typology including children leaving home; descriptive, no effect estimated.
Conceptual and methodological critique of the extended-family-raises-fertility proposition, and explicitly notes the scarcity of evidence. Directly on this chapter's cell as framing, no estimate.
Analytic model of how mortality, fertility and marriage age determine household size under nuclear, extended and stem systems. Runs the arrow the other way.
Ethnography of daggers and silver cups in Nuristan.
Sibling behavioural outcomes; 'living at home' refers to the index child.
Trends in nuclear versus extended household shares in Japan; establishes the exposure trend, no fertility outcome.
Timing and duration of the leaving-home stage as a function of sibship composition and birth intervals. Australian data, no fertility outcome.
Simulation of stem-family development cycles; residence rules vary, outcome is household composition.
Long-term course of anorexia nervosa.
Korean community-health nursing needs by family development stage.
No abstract, but the title — canonical analysis of innovative consumer behaviour — is decisive on subject.
Korean differential-fertility and family-planning resurvey; family relations are surveyed but no arrangement exposure is estimated.
Same Ichon resurvey as the preceding record, Korean-language version.
Family support to pregnant adolescents, with prospective grandmothers interviewed; whether co-residence is the exposure is not visible in the abstract.
Stem-family domestic development cycles as a link between demographic and social processes; conceptual.
Dataset description, married couples in Oakland; 'children living at home' is a sampling stratum.
Canadian household and family trends including co-residence of family members; descriptive, no fertility estimate.
Clinical essay on the phases of married life.
Marital status and children against global happiness.
Street form and suburban neighbouring; 'children living at home' is a covariate.
Hair zinc in schoolchildren; 'number of children living at home' is a covariate.

REVIEW of the family-type-and-fertility literature, concluding the extended-family-raises-fertility belief is unsupported. Channel 1 was scored as dry; this is the closest thing to a prior review on the extended-household cell and should be read in full.
Historical household size and composition in Åland 1760-1880, including coresident kin; pre-modern and descriptive.
Demo-economic model construction survey; household formation is one endogenised block among eight.
Bulgarian marriage rate and marital fertility during the transition; nuptiality, not the arrangement.
Characteristics of pregnant adolescents; home environment is a descriptive covariate.
No abstract and the title — normal stresses during the transition to parenthood — is not decisive either way.
Pharmacy graduates' practice patterns and stereotyping.
Neighbourhood use dimensions, Detroit.

Model of the peasant household under stem-family institutional rules explaining the onset of Japan's fertility transition. Arrangement rules are the exposure but the paper is a model, and the period is FDT rather than SDT.
Measurement of horizontal tax inequity across living units.
Having had offspring against wellbeing at age 50+; 'no children under 18 living at home' is a sample restriction.

Household formation rules and fertility in pre-transition England over three centuries. Exactly the pre-modern niche mechanism, which Ruling 2 leaves with A.7; carried here as theory and cross-reference.
Korean family life cycle trends 1935-1975 including children leaving home and the empty nest; descriptive.
Irish migration to Britain; late marriage and nuptiality appear as background.
Runs the arrow backwards: the baby boom's age structure driving net household formation and housing demand.
Age structure and development in ASEAN and Japan.
Household composition and housing need; no fertility outcome, and the arrangement is not the exposure.
No abstract; the title — interrole conflict among married women — is decisive on subject.
Hajnal's simple-versus-joint household formation systems. The canonical statement of the pre-modern niche rule; A.7's under Ruling 2, carried here as theory.
Demographic viability of patrilineal bands among hunter-gatherers.
Japanese family structure against married women's employment. The arrangement IS the exposure but the outcome is the job, which is the route-out the scope predicted would be largest.
Brazilian fertility on urbanisation, income and education; no arrangement exposure.
